---
title: "Preliminaries"
lang: en
---

In this chapter we introduce the concepts required for the rest of the
thesis. We present the definition of the central notion of this work — the
partial order — and use it to introduce concepts of interest such as
antichain, maximal antichain, dense subset, and dense subset below an
element of a partial order. We set up the standard language of forcing
theory and state its fundamental theorems. Finally, we exhibit some
examples and properties of partial orders.

## Partial orders

::: {#def-orden-parcial}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a set, $\leq$ a binary relation on $\mathbb P$, and
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$ an element of $\mathbb P$. We say that
$(\mathbb P, \leq, \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$ is a **partial order** if and
only if for every $p, q, r \in \mathbb P$ the following hold:

1. $\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$ is the unique element of $\mathbb P$ that
   satisfies $p \leq \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$ for every $p \in \mathbb P$.
2. $p \leq p$.
3. If $p \leq q$ and $q \leq r$, then $p \leq r$.
:::

According to the previous definition, $\mathbb P \neq \emptyset$ and
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$ is a maximum element of $\mathbb P$. From now on,
all our partial orders will have a maximum element $\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$.
The relation mentioned is not necessarily antisymmetric (i.e. $p \leq q$
and $q \leq p$ do not necessarily imply $p = q$). When the relation does
satisfy antisymmetry, we will say that the partial order in question is an
*antisymmetric partial order*. It is common to find in the literature what
is here defined as a partial order called a *preorder*. In this sense, for
the purposes of this work preorder means the same thing as partial order.

For notational simplicity, whenever we speak of the partial order
$\mathbb P$ we shall be referring to the triple
$(\mathbb P, \leq, \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$. In this context, the symbol
$\mathbb P$ will always denote a partial order (or forcing notion) and,
whenever there is no risk of confusion, we will write $\mathbb{1}$ instead
of $\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$ for the maximum element of $\mathbb P$.

::: {#def-compatibilidad}
Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$.

1. We say that $p$ and $q$ are **compatible** $(p \mid q)$ if there is
   $r \in \mathbb P$ such that $r \leq p$ and $r \leq q$.
2. $p$ and $q$ are **incompatible** $(p \perp q)$ if they are not
   compatible — that is, if there is no $r \in \mathbb P$ such that
   $r \leq p$ and $r \leq q$.
:::

Note that any two comparable elements are always compatible. In other
words, if $p, q \in \mathbb P$ and $p \leq q$, then $p \mid q$ as an
immediate consequence of the previous definition. So, for example, we
always have $p \mid \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$. On the other hand, when two
elements of $\mathbb P$ are comparable ($p \leq q$) we say that $p$ is an
*extension* of $q$, and consequently, when two elements of $\mathbb P$ are
compatible we say that they *admit a common extension*.

::: {#def-anticadena}
Let $A, X \subseteq \mathbb P$.

1. $A$ is an **antichain** if any two distinct elements of $A$ are
   incompatible.
2. $A \subseteq X$ is a **maximal antichain in** $X$ if $A$ is an
   antichain and no other antichain in $X$ contains it properly.
:::

Observe that if $A \subseteq \mathbb P$ is an antichain and
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P} \in A$, then $A = \{\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}\}$. This
follows because $\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P} \mid p$ for every $p \in \mathbb P$.

::: {#def-anticadena-trivial}
$A \subseteq \mathbb P$ is the **trivial antichain** if
$A = \{\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}\}$.
:::

When we want to show that a given antichain is maximal, we will do so via
the following equivalence.

::: {#prp-equivalencia}
Let $X \subseteq \mathbb P$. The following are equivalent for any
antichain $A \subseteq X$.

1. $A$ is maximal in $X$.
2. For every $x \in X$ there is $a \in A$ such that $x$ and $a$ are
   compatible.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove this proposition by contrapositive in both directions. Let
$A \subseteq X$ be an antichain. Suppose there is $x \in X$ such that
$x \perp a$ for every $a \in A$. From this, $x \notin A$. Hence
$A \cup \{x\}$ is an antichain that properly contains $A$, so $A$ is not
maximal.

Suppose $A$ is not maximal in $X$. Then there is an antichain
$B \subseteq X$ with $A \varsubsetneq B$. Let $b \in B \setminus A$. Since
$B$ is an antichain, $a \perp b$ for every $a \in A$.
:::

::: {#cor-anticadena-trivial-maximal}
If $A$ is the trivial antichain, then $A$ is maximal in $\mathbb P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $A = \{\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}\}$ and let $p \in \mathbb P$. Then
$p \mid \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$. So, by @prp-equivalencia, $A$ is maximal
in $\mathbb P$.
:::

We now introduce the concepts of a dense subset of a partial order and a
dense subset below an element of a partial order. Both will be of
particular relevance in the next section.

::: {#def-denso}
If $D \subseteq \mathbb P$ and $p_0 \in \mathbb P$, then:

1. $D$ is a **dense subset** of $\mathbb P$ if for every $p \in \mathbb P$
   there is $d \in D$ such that $d \leq p$.
2. $D$ is **dense below** $p_0$ if for every $r \leq p_0$ there is
   $d \in D$ such that $d \leq r$.
:::

A first consequence of being a dense subset of a partial order is that it
suffices for an antichain to be maximal in the dense set in order to be
maximal in the whole order — a fact we prove next.

::: {#prp-amaximalendenso}
If $D$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb P$, then every maximal antichain in
$D$ is maximal in $\mathbb P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $p \in \mathbb P$ and let $A \subseteq D$ be a maximal antichain in
$D$. Then, for some $d \in D$, $d \leq p$ since $D$ is dense in $\mathbb P$.
By @prp-equivalencia, $d \mid a$ for some $a \in A$. Let $q \leq d, a$.
Then $q \leq p, a$. We have shown that every element of $\mathbb P$ is
compatible with some element of $A$ — that is, $A$ is maximal in
$\mathbb P$.
:::

Up to this point we have spoken of the properties of maximal antichains,
but we have not shown that they exist. The next result repairs this gap.

::: {#prp-extenderanticadenamaximal}
If $B \subseteq X \subseteq \mathbb P$ and $B$ is an antichain, then there
is a maximal antichain in $X$ that contains $B$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We want to see that $B$ can be extended to a maximal antichain in $X$. To
that end, consider the following set:
$$
\Sigma = \{A \subseteq X : A \text{ is an antichain and } B \subseteq A\}.
$$

We check that the partial order $(\Sigma, \subseteq)$ satisfies the
hypotheses of Zorn's Lemma. $\Sigma \neq \emptyset$ because $B \in \Sigma$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be any non-empty chain in $\Sigma$. We show that
$\bigcup \mathcal C$ is an upper bound in $\Sigma$ for $\mathcal C$.

For every $A \in \mathcal C$, $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal C$. Let
$x \in \bigcup \mathcal C$. Then $x \in A$ for some $A \in \mathcal C$ and,
since $\mathcal C$ is a chain of elements in $\Sigma$, $A \subseteq X$ and
therefore $x \in X$.

Now, $\bigcup \mathcal C$ is an antichain: if
$x, y \in \bigcup \mathcal C$ are distinct, then there exist
$A_0, A_1 \in \mathcal C$ such that $x \in A_0$ and $y \in A_1$. Since
$\mathcal C$ is a chain, either $A_0 \subseteq A_1$ or $A_1 \subseteq A_0$.
Suppose $A_0 \subseteq A_1$; then $x$ and $y$ are both elements of $A_1$,
which is an antichain, and therefore $x \perp y$. The argument is
analogous if $A_1 \subseteq A_0$.

To verify that $\bigcup \mathcal C$ contains $B$, note that since
$\mathcal C \neq \emptyset$, there is $A \in \mathcal C$ with
$A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal C$. Then $A \in \Sigma$, hence
$B \subseteq A$, and therefore $B \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal C$.

In summary, every non-empty chain in $\Sigma$ has an upper bound in
$\Sigma$, and so by Zorn's Lemma there is $A \subseteq \mathbb P$ that is
a maximal element of $\Sigma$.
:::

## Generic extensions

For the rest of this work, $V$ will always denote a countable transitive
model of a sufficiently large fragment of the ZFC axioms — that is, we
will think of $V$ as a model of those axioms of set theory required to
prove the theorem at hand. Recall that, by Gödel's Second Incompleteness
Theorem, it is not possible to produce within ZFC a model of all the
axioms of ZFC. However, it is possible to consider a countable transitive
model $V$ of any finite list of ZFC axioms. We will call $V$ the *ground
model*.

One of the important issues in the development of this work is the need
for certain sets to be elements of the ground model. To deal with this we
must turn to the concept of *relativization*. Given the breadth and
complexity of the topic, we refer the reader to [@kunen, IV §2] for
further details. We present below an example of a typical situation that
will arise throughout the text and that illustrates how to argue when a
set belongs to the ground model $V$:

Assume $\{\mathbb P, \leq\} \subseteq V$. Given $X \in V$ with
$X \subseteq \mathbb P$, define the formula
$$
\varphi : \forall x \in X \, (p \perp x).
$$

We wish to argue that if
$Y = \{p \in \mathbb P : \varphi(p)\}
   = \{p \in \mathbb P : \forall x \in X \, (p \perp x)\}$,
then $Y \in V$; to do so we show that $\varphi$ is absolute for $V$ —
that is, $\varphi$ is equivalent to $\varphi^V$, the relativization of
$\varphi$ to $V$. We begin by observing that, given
$p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \perp q$ means
$\neg \exists r \, (r \in \mathbb P \,\&\, r \leq p \,\&\, r \leq q)$.
Moreover, $r \leq p$ and $r \leq q$ mean $(r, p) \in \,\leq$ and
$(r, q) \in \,\leq$.

Since $p, q \in \mathbb P \in V$ and $V$ is a transitive model, we have
$p, q \in V$. Then $(p \leq q)^V$ if and only if $p \leq q$ because $\in$
is absolute (see [@kunen, VI §3]) and $\leq \, \in V$. Hence
$(p \perp q)^V \leftrightarrow p \perp q$. In conclusion,
$\{p \in \mathbb P : \varphi^V(p)\} = Y$. Therefore $Y \in V$.

In general we will skip the details whenever the notions involved are
absolute and the parameters are elements of $V$. For instance, in the
previous case we will simply say that $Y \in V$ because
$\mathbb P, X \in V$, where, from now on, $\mathbb P \in V$ will mean that
$\{\mathbb P, \leq\} \subseteq V$.

::: {#def-filtro}
Let $G \subseteq \mathbb P$ be non-empty. We will say that $G$ is a
**filter** on $\mathbb P$ if the following hold:

1. whenever $p \in G$ and $q \in \mathbb P$, $p \leq q$ implies $q \in G$;
   and
2. if $p, q \in G$, then there is $r \in G$ such that $r \leq p, q$.
:::

Note that since $G \neq \emptyset$ and $p \leq \mathbb{1}$ for every
$p \in G$, it follows from clause (1) of the previous definition that
$\mathbb{1}$ is always an element of $G$.

We now show that, for any finite subset of a filter, the filter contains a
common extension of all its members.

::: {#prp-extensionparamuchos}
If $G$ is a filter and $F$ is a finite subset of $G$, then there is
$p \in G$ such that $p \leq q$ for every $q \in F$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $F = \{q_0, q_1, \ldots, q_{n-1}\}$. Since $G$ is a filter, there is
$p_0 \in G$ such that $p_0 \leq q_0, q_1$. But then there is $p_1 \in G$
such that $p_1 \leq p_0, q_1$. Continuing in this fashion, there is
$p_{k+1} \in G$ such that $p_{k+1} \leq p_k, q_{k+1}$ for
$k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-2$. Then $p = p_{n-1} \in G$ and $p \leq q$ for
every $q \in F$.
:::

Throughout this work we will be interested in filters that do not avoid
any dense subset of $\mathbb P$ that belongs to the ground model. We make
this precise next.

::: {#def-filtrogenerico}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$. We say that $G \subseteq \mathbb P$ is a
**$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter** if $G$ is a filter and, for every set
$D$ dense in $\mathbb P$, $D \in V$ implies $G \cap D \neq \emptyset$.
:::

The next lemma simplifies the task of verifying that a filter is
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic, and will be used in a later chapter.

::: {#lem-filtroequivalencia}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ and $G \subseteq \mathbb P$. Then $G$ is a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter if and only if for every
$p, q \in \mathbb P$:

1. if $p, q \in G$, then there is $r \in \mathbb P$ such that
   $r \leq p, q$;
2. if $p \in G$ and $p \leq q$, then $q \in G$; and
3. for every $D \subseteq \mathbb P$, if $D \in V$ and $D$ is dense in
   $\mathbb P$, then $G \cap D \neq \emptyset$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter. Since $G$ is a filter,
properties (1) and (2) hold trivially. Property (3) follows from the
genericity of $G$.

We prove the remaining implication. Suppose $G$ satisfies (1), (2), and
(3). By @def-filtrogenerico, it remains to show that any two elements of
$G$ are compatible in $G$. Note that property (1) only guarantees that
any two elements of $G$ admit a common extension in $\mathbb P$. Let
$p, q \in G$. Define
$$
D = \{r \in \mathbb P : r \perp p \,\vee\, r \perp q \,\vee\,
       (r \leq p \,\&\, r \leq q)\}.
$$

We show that $D$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb P$. Let $s \in \mathbb P$.
If for some $r \leq s$ we have $r$ incompatible with $p$ or with $q$,
then $r \leq s$ and $r \in D$. If, on the contrary, every extension of
$s$ is compatible with both $p$ and $q$, then there is
$r_0 \in \mathbb P$ such that $r_0 \leq s, p$ (since $s \leq s$). Then
there is $r \in \mathbb P$ such that $r \leq r_0, q$, since $r_0 \leq s$.
Hence $r \leq p, q$ — that is, $r$ is an extension of $s$ in $D$.

Now, by hypothesis $\mathbb P \in V$, and by the transitivity of $V$,
$p, q \in V$. Thus $D \in V$. By property (3),
$G \cap D \neq \emptyset$. Let $r \in G \cap D$. Note that we cannot have
$r \perp p$ nor $r \perp q$, since otherwise $G$ would contain two
incompatible elements, contradicting property (1). Therefore $r \in G$
and $r \leq p, q$.
:::

The reason we require our models of ZFC to be countable can be seen in
the proof of the next result.

::: {#lem-condicionenG}
If $\mathbb P \in V$, then for every $p \in \mathbb P$ there is a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$ such that $p \in G$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\langle D_n : n \in \omega \rangle$ be an enumeration of all dense
subsets of $\mathbb P$ that belong to $V$. By the density of each $D_n$,
we may inductively choose $q_{n+1} \in D_n$ so that the sequence
$\langle q_i : i < \omega \rangle$ is decreasing. In other words, there
is a sequence $\langle q_i : i < \omega \rangle$ such that:

- $q_0 = p$
- $q_{n+1} \leq q_n$ with $q_{n+1} \in D_n$

Now consider $G = \{r \in \mathbb P : \exists n \, (q_n \leq r)\}$. We
show that $G$ is the desired set. Let $r, s \in G$. Then there are
$n, m \in \omega$ such that $q_n \leq r$ and $q_m \leq s$. Without loss
of generality, suppose $n \leq m$. Then $q_m \leq r, s$ and $q_m \in G$.

Let $s \in \mathbb P$ and $r \in G$ with $r \leq s$. Then $q_n \leq r$
for some $n \in \omega$. So $q_n \leq s$, hence $s \in G$.

$G$ is generic because $q_{n+1} \in G \cap D_n$ for every $n$.
:::

We now turn to partial orders in which every element admits two
mutually-incompatible extensions.

::: {#def-ordennoatomico}
We say that $\mathbb P$ is **atomless** if for every $p \in \mathbb P$
there are $r, q \in \mathbb P$ such that $r, q \leq p$ and $r \perp q$.
:::

The importance of atomless partial orders is that they produce proper
extensions of the ground model, as the next result shows.

::: {#lem-noatomico}
If $\mathbb P \in V$ is atomless and $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic
filter, then $G \notin V$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose, on the contrary, that $G \in V$. Then
$D = \mathbb P \setminus G \in V$, since set difference is an absolute
notion. $D$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb P$: if $p \in \mathbb P$, then
there are $r, q \in \mathbb P$ that are mutually incompatible extensions
of $p$. Note that $r$ and $q$ cannot both be in $G$, since $r \perp q$
and $G$ is a filter. Hence $r \leq p$ and $r \in D$, or $q \leq p$ and
$q \in D$. But then $D$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb P$ with $D \in V$
and $G \cap D = \emptyset$, contradicting the genericity of $G$.
:::

From now on, all our partial orders will be atomless (in some cases we
will say *atom-free partial order* instead of atomless).

A central concept for talking about a model that will turn out to be an
extension of $V$ is the following:

::: {#def-pnombre}
$\dot x$ is a **$\mathbb P$-name** if and only if $\dot x$ is a relation
and for every $(\dot y, p) \in \dot x$ we have that $\dot y$ is a
$\mathbb P$-name and $p \in \mathbb P$.
:::

The previous definition is given recursively. The Axiom of Foundation
(also called the Axiom of Regularity) guarantees that this definition
makes sense. Note moreover that the definition is given in terms of
absolute concepts, so the notion of $\mathbb P$-name is absolute.

::: {#def-vp}
We denote by $V^{\mathbb P}$ the collection of all $\mathbb P$-names that
belong to $V$.
:::

The collection just defined becomes relevant once we have a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$, since the inhabitants of the model
that we are pursuing — which will extend $V$ — turn out to be the
valuations of the elements of $V^{\mathbb P}$ with respect to $G$. We
make this precise with the next two definitions.

::: {#def-valuacion}
If $\dot x \in V^{\mathbb P}$ and $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic
filter, we define the **valuation** of $\dot x$ with respect to $G$
recursively as
$$
\dot x_G = \{\dot y_G : \exists p \in G \, ((\dot y, p) \in \dot x)\}.
$$
:::

::: {#def-vg}
If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, we define
$$
V[G] = \{\dot x_G : \dot x \in V^{\mathbb P}\}.
$$
:::

One way to read $V[G]$ is as follows: $x$ belongs to $V[G]$ if and only
if $x$ is definable in $V[G]$ from $G$ and finitely many elements of $V$,
and therefore has a name.

A crucial fact is that $V[G]$ turns out to be the smallest extension that
contains $V$:

::: {#lem-minimalidad}
If $M$ is a transitive model of ZFC with $V \subseteq M$ and $G \in M$,
then $V[G] \subseteq M$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For every $\dot x \in V^{\mathbb P}$, $\dot x \in M$ and $G \in M$. Thus
$\dot x_G = (\dot x_G)^M \in M$, where $(\dot x_G)^M$ is the
relativization of the set $\dot x_G$ to the model $M$ (see [@kunen, VII]).
:::

The next theorem, together with @lem-minimalidad, establishes that
$V[G]$ is a transitive model of ZFC containing $V$. Its proof is omitted
as it exceeds the scope of this thesis. The reader is referred to the
proof developed throughout [@kunen, VII §2] and [@kunen, VII Theorem 4.2].

::: {#thm-vg-es-modelo}
If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then $V[G]$ is a countable
transitive model of ZFC with $V \subseteq V[G]$.
:::

The next definition and @lem-valuacioncanonica show that any element of
$V$ can be represented in canonical form by a name, which we will denote
by $\check{x}$.

::: {#def-nombrecanonico}
We define the **canonical $\mathbb P$-name** of $x \in V$ recursively by
$$
\check{x} = \{(\check{y}, \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}) : y \in x\}.
$$
:::

Note that, formally, $\check{x}$ depends on the maximum element
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$ as well as on $x$. The set $\mathbb P$ will
always be clear from context. The previous definition is recursive and
uses only absolute concepts, so if $x \in V$ then $\check{x} \in V$. A
relevant fact is that the valuation of $\check{x}$ with respect to a
generic filter $G$ turns out to be $x$. This is the content of the
following lemma (see a proof in [@kunen, VII Lemma 2.11]):

::: {#lem-valuacioncanonica}
If $\mathbb P \in V$ and $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then
for every $x \in V$ we have $\check{x} \in V^{\mathbb P}$ and
$\check{x}_G = x$.
:::

It is of interest to know whether there is a name whose valuation with
respect to $G$ is precisely the generic filter. This is answered by the
next definition and lemma.

::: {#def-gamma}
Given $\mathbb P \in V$, define
$\Gamma = \{(\check{p}, p) : p \in \mathbb P\}$.
:::

Note that the definition of $\Gamma$ depends on $\mathbb P$. Now,
$\Gamma \in V$ because $\mathbb P \in V$.

::: {#lem-gammaesg}
If $\mathbb P \in V$ and $G \subseteq \mathbb P$ is a non-empty filter,
then $\Gamma_G = G$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$\Gamma_G = \{\check{p}_G : p \in G\} = \{p : p \in G\} = G$.
:::

By the previous lemma, there is a name, $\Gamma$, whose valuation with
respect to $G$ returns $G$. This lets us conclude that $G \in V[G]$.

Combining this observation with @thm-vg-es-modelo, $V[G]$ is the smallest
transitive extension containing $V$ as a set and $G$ as an element.

::: {#lem-lemadenso}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ and let $E \subseteq \mathbb P$ with $E \in V$. For
every $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$ we have:

1. $G \cap E \neq \emptyset$, or there is $q \in G$ such that $r \perp q$
   for every $r \in E$.
2. If $p \in G$ and $E$ is dense below $p$, then
   $G \cap E \neq \emptyset$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1). Let $E^{\downarrow} = \{p \in \mathbb P : \exists r \in E \,
(p \leq r)\}$ and $E^{\perp} = \{q \in \mathbb P : \forall r \in E \,
(r \perp q)\}$, and consider $D = E^{\downarrow} \cup E^{\perp}$. We
claim that $D$ is dense in $\mathbb P$. Let $p_0 \in \mathbb P$. If
$p_0 \in E^{\perp}$, then $p_0$ is an element of $D$ that extends itself
and we are done. Otherwise $p_0 \notin E^{\perp}$, so there is
$r_0 \in E$ with $r_0 \mid p_0$ — that is, $p \leq r_0$ and $p \leq p_0$
for some $p \in \mathbb P$. But then $p \in E^{\downarrow}$, hence $p$ is
an element of $D$ extending $p_0$.

Now, $D \in V$ since $\mathbb P, E \in V$. Since $G$ is
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic, $G \cap D \neq \emptyset$. Let
$p \in G \cap D$. If $p \in E^{\downarrow}$, then $p \leq r$ for some
$r \in E$, which implies $r \in G$ since $p \in G$ and $G$ is a filter.
Thus $G \cap E \neq \emptyset$. If $p \in E^{\perp}$, then $p \in G$ is
incompatible with every element of $E$, which finishes the proof.

(2). By contradiction. Suppose that for some $p \in G$ with $E$ dense
below $p$, $G \cap E = \emptyset$. By (1) there is then some $q \in G$
incompatible with every element of $E$. Since $G$ is a filter, there is
$t \in G$ such that $t \leq p, q$. Since $E$ is dense below $p$,
$r \leq t$ for some $r \in E$, hence $r \leq q$ and in particular
$r \mid q$, which is impossible.
:::

The next lemma shows that generic filters are maximal in the sense of
containment.

::: {#lem-filtrosiguales}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$. If $G$ and $H$ are both $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic
filters and $G \subseteq H$, then $G = H$.
:::

::: {.proof}
It remains to show $H \subseteq G$. By contradiction, suppose there is
$p \in H \setminus G$. Then $G \cap \{p\} = \emptyset$. By
@lem-lemadenso (1) applied to $G$ and $\{p\}$, there is
$q \in G \subseteq H$ such that $q \perp p$, which is impossible because
$H$ is a filter.
:::

## Forcing

Let us now set up our main relation of interest in this section: the
forcing relation. Relaxing notation for a moment, the symbol
$p \Vdash \phi$ should be read as "$p$ *forces* $\phi$".

::: {#def-forzar}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ and let $\varphi(y_1, \ldots, y_n)$ be a formula
whose free variables are $y_1, \ldots, y_n$. Let
$\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n \in V^{\mathbb P}$ and $p \in \mathbb P$. We
say that $p \Vdash \varphi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$ if and only if
for every $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$ with $p \in G$,
$\varphi^{V[G]}((\dot x_1)_G, \ldots, (\dot x_n)_G)$ holds.
:::

The next lemma will be very useful in later proofs; its proof can be
consulted in [@kunen, VII Lemma 3.2]. Informally, clause (1) says that
if $p \in \mathbb P$ and $p \Vdash \phi$, then every extension of $p$
also forces $\phi$; clause (2) says that if $p$ forces two formulas, then
$p$ forces their conjunction.

::: {#lem-alguienmasfuerte}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ and $\phi(y_1, \ldots, y_n)$ a formula whose free
variables are $y_1, \ldots, y_n$. Let
$\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n \in V^{\mathbb P}$ and $p, q \in \mathbb P$.
The following hold.

1. If $p \Vdash \phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$ and $q \leq p$, then
   $q \Vdash \phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$.
2. $(p \Vdash \phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n))$ and
   $(p \Vdash \psi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n))$ if and only if
   $p \Vdash (\phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n) \,\&\,
              \psi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n))$.
:::

The next theorem is the most important result in the basic theory of
forcing. By @def-forzar, if $\varphi$ is a formula, the notion
$p \Vdash \varphi$ requires knowledge of all generic filters $G$ —
meaning the forcing notion has been defined in terms of objects external
to $V$. However, the first thing the theorem establishes is that one can
define a notion equivalent to $\Vdash$, denoted $\Vdash^*$, definable by
a formula that admits a relativization to $V$. The second thing it
establishes is that if $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then
$\varphi$ holds in $V[G]$ iff there is a condition in $G$ that forces
$\varphi$. Informally, "something" happens in the generic extension if
and only if some element of the filter $G$ forces it to happen. As the
proof does not contribute substantively to the development of this
thesis we omit it; a demonstration can be found in
[@kunen, VII Theorem 3.6].

::: {#thm-teoremadeforcing}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ and $\phi(y_1, \ldots, y_n)$ a formula whose free
variables are $y_1, \ldots, y_n$. Let
$\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n \in V^{\mathbb P}$. The following hold.

1. For every $p \in \mathbb P$,
   $p \Vdash \phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n) \leftrightarrow
    (p \Vdash^{*} \phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n))^V$.
2. For every $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$,
$$
\phi((\dot x_1)_G, \ldots, (\dot x_n)_G)^{V[G]}
\;\text{if and only if there is}\; p \in G \;\text{such that}\;
p \Vdash \phi(\dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n).
$$
:::

The next result will be very useful in the section on composition of
forcing notions. A clarification: as we have said, a $\mathbb P$-name is
a binary relation and thus every $\mathbb P$-name $\dot X$ has a domain
(the set of all first coordinates of $\dot X$). The proof of clause (1)
is omitted; a proof can be found in [@kunen, VII Corollary 3.7].

::: {#lem-nombreeneldominio}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ and let
$\dot X, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n \in V^{\mathbb P}$. Let
$\phi(y_0, \ldots, y_n)$ be a formula whose free variables are
$y_0, \ldots, y_n$. If $p \in \mathbb P$ and
$p \Vdash \exists x \, (x \in \dot X \,\&\,
\phi(x, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n))$, then:

1. There are $r \in \mathbb P$ and
   $\dot x \in \operatorname{dom} \dot X$ such that $r \leq p$ and
   $r \Vdash \phi(\dot x, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$.
2. If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter and $p \in G$, then
   there are $r \in G$ and $\dot x \in \operatorname{dom} \dot X$ such
   that $r \leq p$ and $r \Vdash \phi(\dot x, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Define $D = \{s \in \mathbb P : \exists \dot x \in \operatorname{dom}
\dot X \, (s \Vdash \phi(\dot x, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n))\}$. We
show that $D$ is dense below $p$. Let $p_1 \leq p$. By (1), there are
$s \leq p_1$ and $\dot x \in \operatorname{dom} \dot X$ such that
$s \Vdash \phi(\dot x, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$. So $s \leq p_1$ and
$s \in D$.

Now, on the one hand $D$ is defined in terms of $\mathbb P$ and
$\operatorname{dom} \dot X$ — sets that are elements of $V$. On the
other hand, $D$ is also defined in terms of $\Vdash$, which by
@thm-teoremadeforcing (1) is equivalent to $\Vdash^*$, a notion that can
be relativized to $V$. Hence $D \in V$. By @lem-lemadenso (2),
$G \cap D \neq \emptyset$. Let $s \in G \cap D$. Then $s \in G$ and
there is $\dot x \in \operatorname{dom} \dot X$ such that
$s \Vdash \phi(\dot x, \dot x_1, \ldots, \dot x_n)$. Let $r \in G$ with
$r \leq p, s$. By @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$r \Vdash \phi(\dot x, \dot x_1, \ldots, x_n)$.
:::

## Examples

The forcing notions and properties of forcing notions in this section
will be used extensively throughout the rest of this work.

::: {#def-fn}
For any pair of sets $I$ and $J$, define
$$
\operatorname{Fn}(I, J) = \{p : |p| < \omega \,\&\,
                                p \text{ is a function} \,\&\,
                                p \subseteq I \times J\}.
$$

We order $\operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$ by: $p \leq q$ if and only if
$q \subseteq p$.
:::

The next lemma gives a compatibility criterion for elements of
$\operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$.

::: {#lem-unionesfuncion}
Let $p, q \in \operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$. Then $p$ is compatible with $q$
if and only if $p \cup q$ is a function.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $p$ and $q$ are compatible. Then, by the order on
$\operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$, $p \subseteq r$ and $q \subseteq r$ for some
$r \in \operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$. So $p \cup q \subseteq r$ and the result
follows.

Suppose now that $p \cup q$ is a function. Since
$p \subseteq p \cup q$ and $q \subseteq p \cup q$, $p \cup q$ is a common
extension of $p$ and $q$ in $\operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$, hence they are
compatible.
:::

::: {#def-concatenacion}
For every ordinal $\alpha$:

1. $p \in 2^{<\alpha}$ if and only if there is an ordinal $\beta < \alpha$
   such that $p : \beta \to \{0, 1\}$.
2. $2^{<\alpha}$ is ordered by $p \leq q$ if and only if $q \subseteq p$.
3. If $p \in 2^{<\alpha}$, we define, for each $i < 2$,
   $p^\frown i := p \cup \{(\operatorname{dom} p, i)\}$.
:::

Analogously we define the following.

::: {#def-omegafinito}
$\omega^{<\omega} := \{p : \exists n < \omega \,
                              (p : n \to \omega)\}$.
:::

For the rest of this work, $2^{<\alpha}$ and $\omega^{<\omega}$ will
denote, respectively, the triples $(2^{<\alpha}, \leq, \emptyset)$ and
$(\omega^{<\omega}, \leq, \emptyset)$, where $\leq$ is the order defined
above and $\emptyset$ is the maximum element of both sets. We call
$\omega^{<\omega}$ **Cohen forcing**.

Observe that, by @def-concatenacion, if $p \in 2^{<\alpha}$ and
$\operatorname{dom} p + 1 < \alpha$, then
$p^\frown i \in 2^{<\alpha}$ and
$\operatorname{dom}(p^\frown i) = \operatorname{dom} p + 1$. This shows
that if $p \in 2^{<\alpha}$, then $p^{\frown}0$ and $p^{\frown}1$ are
mutually-incompatible extensions of $p$ — that is, $2^{<\alpha}$ is
atomless. Note also that if @lem-unionesfuncion is restated with
$2^{<\alpha}$ in place of $\operatorname{Fn}(I, J)$, the same argument
shows that two elements in $2^{<\alpha}$ are compatible if and only if
their union is a function.

If we take $\alpha = \omega$ in the last definition, then $2^{<\omega}$
is defined in terms of absolute notions (see
[@kunen, Theorem 5.1, p. 126] for details), which lets us conclude that
$2^{<\omega} \in V$ — a fact relevant to the next proposition.

::: {#prp-unnuevoreal}
If $G$ is a $(V, 2^{<\omega})$-generic filter and $g = \bigcup G$, then:

1. $g : \omega \to 2$.
2. $G = \{g \restriction n : n \in \omega\}$.
3. $g \in V[G] \setminus V$.
:::

::: {.proof}
To simplify notation, let $\mathbb P = 2^{<\omega}$. We show that
$g = \bigcup G$ is a function from $\omega$ to $2$. Since any two
elements of $G$ are compatible, $g$ is a function (see
@lem-unionesfuncion). Note that
$\operatorname{dom} g = \bigcup_{p \in G} \operatorname{dom} p$, so
$\operatorname{dom} g \subseteq \omega$.

Let $n \in \omega$ be arbitrary; we show $n \in \operatorname{dom} g$.
Define $D_n = \{p \in \mathbb P : n \in \operatorname{dom} p\}$. We show
that $D_n$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb P$. Let $p \in \mathbb P$. If
$n \in \operatorname{dom} p$, then $p \in D_n$ and, since $p \leq p$, the
result follows. If $n \notin \operatorname{dom} p$, consider
$r : n + 1 \to 2$ defined by
$$
r(i) = \begin{cases} p(i), & \text{if } i \in \operatorname{dom} p, \\
                     0,    & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Then $r$ is a function in $D_n$ that extends $p$. So $D_n$ is dense in
$\mathbb P$. Since $\mathbb P \in V$ and $\operatorname{dom} p$ is
definable in $V$, $D_n \in V$. Hence $G \cap D_n \neq \emptyset$. Let
$p \in G \cap D_n$. Then $p \in G$ and $n \in \operatorname{dom} p$. So
$n \in \operatorname{dom} g$.

The left-to-right containment of (2) holds because if $p \in G$, since
$\operatorname{dom} p \in \omega$,
$p = g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p$. It remains to show that for
every $n \in \omega$, $g \restriction n \in G$. By what was shown in (1),
$D_n$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb P$ with $D_n \in V$, so
$G \cap D_n \neq \emptyset$. Let $p \in G \cap D_n$. Then
$n < \operatorname{dom} p$, hence
$g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p \leq g \restriction n$. Since
$g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p = p$ and $p \in G$, we have
$g \restriction n \in G$.

We prove $g \in V[G] \setminus V$ by contradiction. If $g \in V$, then by
(2), $G \in V$, contradicting @lem-noatomico.
:::

The function $g$ in the previous theorem is called a **Cohen real** and,
by clause (3), one customarily says that a new Cohen real has been
*added*.

In contrast to the previous proposition, the next result shows that one
can consider a partial order $\mathbb P \in V$ such that, given a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$, the generic extension $V[G]$
contains no new functions from $\omega$ to $2$. For this we take
$\mathbb P = (2^{<\omega_1})^V$ — that is, $\mathbb P$ is the partial
order that $V$ thinks consists of functions from an ordinal less than
$\omega_1^V$ to $2$.

::: {#prp-nadanuevo}
If $\mathbb P = (2^{<\omega_1})^V$ and $G$ is a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then $V[G]$ contains no new functions
from $\omega$ to $2$ — that is,
$V[G] \cap {}^{\omega}2 \subseteq V$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $f \in V[G] \cap {}^{\omega}2$. By @def-vg, there is
$\dot f \in V^{\mathbb P}$ such that $\dot f_G = f$. Now, by
@thm-teoremadeforcing (2), some $p \in G$ satisfies
$p \Vdash \dot f : \check \omega \to \check 2$. Consider the formula
$\varphi(r) : r \in \mathbb P \,\&\, \exists h \in {}^{\omega}2 \,
(r \Vdash \dot f = \check h)$. Since $\mathbb P \in V$ and the notions
${}^{\omega}2$ and $\Vdash$ can be relativized to $V$, the formula
$\varphi$ can be relativized to $V$.

Define $D = \{r \in \mathbb P : \varphi^V(r)\}$. Note that $D \in V$. We
show that $D$ is dense below $p$. From this point on we work in $V$ —
i.e. the following arguments are to be understood as relativized to $V$.
Let $p_0 \leq p$. By @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$p_0 \Vdash \dot f : \check \omega \to \check 2$. In particular,
$p_0 \Vdash \exists x \, (x \in \check 2 \,\&\,
\dot f(\check 0) = x)$. By @lem-nombreeneldominio (1), there are
$p_1 \in \mathbb P$ and $\dot y \in \operatorname{dom} \check 2$ with
$p_1 \leq p_0$ and $p_1 \Vdash \dot f(\check 0) = \dot y$. Now, recall
$\check 2 = \{(\check z, \emptyset) : z \in 2\}$, so
$\dot y \in \operatorname{dom} \check 2$ implies $\dot y = \check m_0$
for some $m_0 \in 2$ — that is,
$p_1 \Vdash \dot f(\check 0) = \check m_0$. Since
$p_1 \leq p_0 \leq p$, by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$p_1 \Vdash \dot f : \check \omega \to \check 2$. In particular,
$p_1 \Vdash \exists x \, (x \in \check 2 \,\&\,
\dot f(\check 1) = x)$. Applying @lem-nombreeneldominio (1) again, there
are $p_2 \leq p_1$ and $m_1 \in 2$ with
$p_2 \Vdash \dot f(\check 1) = \check m_1$. This procedure produces two
sequences, $\{p_k : k < \omega\} \subseteq \mathbb P$ and
$\{m_k : k < \omega\}$, such that for every $k < \omega$:
$p_{k+1} \leq p_k$, $m_k \in 2$, and
$p_{k+1} \Vdash \dot f(\check k) = \check m_k$. Let
$r = \bigcup_{n \in \omega} p_n$. Since $p_{k+1} \leq p_k$,
$p_{k+1} \mid p_k$. Thus $r$ is the union of compatible functions, so
$r$ is a function (see @lem-unionesfuncion). Moreover
$\operatorname{dom} r = \bigcup_{n \in \omega} \operatorname{dom} p_n$,
where $\operatorname{dom} p_n < \omega_1$. Hence
$\operatorname{dom} r < \omega_1$, so $r \in \mathbb P$. Define
$h : \omega \to 2$ by $h(n) = m_n$. Since $p_0 \subseteq r$ and
$r \Vdash \dot f = \check{h}$, $r \leq p_0$ and $r \in D$.

By @lem-lemadenso (2), $G \cap D \neq \emptyset$ — that is, there are
$r \in G$ and $h \in {}^{\omega}2 \cap V$ such that
$r \Vdash \dot f = \check h$. As a direct consequence of @def-forzar,
$f = \dot f_G = h$, and since $h \in V$, the result follows.
:::

At various points in this work we will be interested in partial orders
$\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ where the first stands in a special relation
to the second.

::: {#def-suborden}
We say that $\mathbb P$ is a **suborder** of $\mathbb Q$ if
$\mathbb P \subseteq \mathbb Q$ and
$\leq_{\mathbb P} \,:=\, \leq_{\mathbb Q} \cap \, (\mathbb P \times \mathbb P)$.
:::

As will be seen in later chapters, a concept that will give us relevant
information is that of an isomorphism between partial orders.

::: {#def-isomorfismo}
Let $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ be two partial orders. We say that
$f : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is an **isomorphism** if $f$ is a bijective
function such that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ preserve the order.
:::

**Notation.** Whenever there is a function between $\mathbb P$ and
$\mathbb Q$ as in the previous definition we write
$\mathbb P \cong \mathbb Q$.
